body.p: I. Claim Status
Claim 4 is amended to address an informality, and claims 12-18 and 31-32 are amended simply to restate the "second section" in a different way. Claims 1-32 remain pending. No new matter is added.
II. The Drawings Are Proper

The Office objects to claim 4 and notes that "to be grammatically correct 'is' should be before 'greater."' Action at 2-3. Claim 4 is amended in the way suggested by the Office. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the objections. IV. The Claims Are Clear
The Office rejections claims 1-32 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as allegedly indefinite. Action at 3-8. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
A. All Claims: "And/Or"

The Office contends that each use of "and/or" in the claims renders all claims indefinite because it is allegedly "unclear whether 1) just one ... or 2) both[/atl]" listed options are required. Action at 3-8. In particular, the Office maintains that, with the use of "and/or," it is "unclear whether":
1. for claims 1 and 24, "just one of the mean curvatures need to be calculated" or
"both mean curvatures need to be calculated" (id. at 3);
2. for claims 3, 8, l 3, 16, 25, 29, 3 l, and 32, the claim "only requires characterizing
whether the patient has multiple sclerosis," "only requires characterizing a type of multiple sclerosis," or requires "both characterizing whether the patient has
multiple sclerosis and the type of multiple sclerosis" (id. at 3-5, 7-8);
3. for claims 3, 4, 8, 25, 26, 29, 31, and 32, "just one mean curvature/rate of change
is required to characterize the patient" or "both mean curvatures/rates of change
are required to characterize the patient" (id. at 3-6);
4. for claims 6 and 27, "just one of the[ recited] ranges is required" or "all of the[
recited] ranges are required" (id.at 6); and
5. for claims 7, 9, 22, and 28, "just one of the[ recited] rates of change is required"
or "both of the[ recited] rates of change are required" (id.at 6-8).

But as the Board has repeatedly held, "and/or" has a clear meaning: when a claim recites A and/or B, it "covers embodiments having element A alone, element B alone, or elements A and B taken together." Ex parte Gross, Appeal No. 2011-004811, slip op. at 4 (PTAB Jan. 3, 2014) (reversing indefiniteness rejection "based on the use of the term 'and/or"'); Ex pane Gomoll, Appeal No. 2011-006816, slip op. at (PTAB Aug. 7, 2013) (reversing indefiniteness rejection contending that "'and/or' ... is indefinite" because the "ordinary of customary meaning of 'and/or' is 'to indicate that two words or expressions are to be taken together or individually"). The use of "and/or" in these claims is thus clear and means
that the claims are broad enough to cover using one or multiple ones of the recited options linked by "and/or"-this "[b]readth is not indefiniteness." In re Gardner, 427 F.2d 786, 788 (CCPA 1970).
B. Independent Claims 1 and 24: Use of Mean Curvature

The Office also implies that claims 1 and 24 are unclear because they recite "determining" or processor(s) configured to determine "a mean curvature of at least a region of a surface of the dorsal portion and/or a mean curvature of at least a region of a surface of the ventral portion" but do not specify how the mean curvature calculations are used such that it is allegedly "unclear what the mean curvature calculations are used for." Action at 3-4. The Office thus "recommends amending the independent claims such that it is clear what the mean curvature is used for within the context of the method and system to analyze the one or more sections of a central nervous system of a patient." Id. But the Office mistakes the breadth of claims 1 and 24-which, without specifying a particular use of the mean curvatures, broadly permit many different uses of thereof-with indefiniteness. "Breadth is not indefiniteness," and the Office has not established that a POSITA would have been unable to ascertain the scope of the actually-recited limitations with reasonable certainty. Gardner, 427 F.2d at 788; Action at 3-4; see, e.g., Ex parte Desabhatla, Appeal No. 2017-005957, slip op. at 2-3 (PTAB Feb. 8, 2018) (claim is not indefinite for failing to specify "the relationship between" recited parameters and what is being determined). The claims are thus clear.
Part"

The Office contends that the recitation of basing a characterization or calculation "at least in part" on recited parameters in claims 3, 8, 9, 11, 13, 16, 23, 25, 29, 31, and 32 "makes it unclear whether" the recited parameters "are actually required in order to" do the characterization or calculation and "what other factors can be included or excluded." Action at 4-5, 7-8. But, as the Board has held, making a determination "based at least in part" on a recited parameter "is not indefinite"-broadly, if a parameter is accounted for in a

determination, the determination can be based at least in part on the parameter, including if other unrecited parameters are also accounted for. See, e.g., Desabhatla, Appeal No. 2017- 005957, slip op. at 2-3 (reversing indefiniteness rejection premised on the use of "based at least in part on" in the claim). Such breadth is not indefiniteness. Id.
Determinations

The Office contends that the claims reciting characterizing or processor(s) configured to characterize "whether the patient has multiple sclerosis and/or a type of multiple sclerosis" are unclear because "it is unclear what happens within the method when the patient does not have multiple sclerosis (i.e. or a type of multiple sclerosis)." Action at 5. The Office also contends that claims 6 and 27 are unclear because "it is unclear what the method does when the mean curvature of the region of the surface of the ventral portion of the first section is not within any of the[ recited] ranges." Id. at 6. But the Office again impermissibly conflates breadth with indefiniteness. Gardner, 427 F.2d at 788. For example, if the characterization of "whether the patient has multiple sclerosis and/or a type of multiple sclerosis" is that the patient does not have multiple sclerosis, then that is the characterization in the recited step-if subsequent steps are not recited, they broadly can (but need not) be performed. Likewise, for claims 6 and 27, if the determination that the mean curvature is not within one of the recited ranges, then that is the determination in the recited step-if subsequent steps are not recited, they broadly can (but need not) be performed. This does not render the claims indefinite. Id.; see, e.g., Desabhatla, Appeal No. 2017-005957, slip op. at 2-3 (no need to specify "the relationship" to satisfy definiteness).
E. Claims 5, 11, 14, 17, 21, andI 25: Patient Ethnicity

The Office contends that claims 5, 14, 17, and 21 are unclear for reciting the ethnicity of the patient-that "the patient is white" or "the patient is Black"-because "it is unclear what the race/ethnicity of the patient is used for," "what impact the race/ethnicity of the patient has on the characterizing," and thus "why an ethnicity/race of the patient is mentioned within the

method claim." Action at 6. And the Office similarly contends that claims 11 and 25 are indefinite for reciting that the characterization is based at least in part on "an ethnicity of the patient" because "[i]t is unclear what impact the race/ethnicity of the patient has on the characterizing." Id. at 7. But claims 5, 14, 17, and 21 merely specify the ethnicity of the patient analyzed in the claimed methods, and a POSITA would have had no issue determining what it means for a patient to be "white" or "Black"-this is enough for definiteness, which merely requires a POSITA to be able to determine "the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty." Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc., 572 U.S. 898, 899 (2014). And, for all claims, Section 112(b) does not require a specification of "what the race/ethnicity of the patient is used for" or the impact thereof "on the characterizing"-since, as noted above, that concerns breadth, not indefiniteness-let alone an explanation for "why" a claim recites particular features.' Gardner, 427 F.2d at 788; Desabhatla, Appeal No. 2017-005957, slip op. at 2-3. These claims are thus also clear.
For at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections.
V. The Claims Recite Patent-Eligible Subject Matter
The Office rejects all claims under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as allegedly reciting patent- ineligible subject matter. Action at 8-13. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
A. Step 2A: The Claims Are Not Directed to a Judicial Exception

The claims are not directed to a judicial exception and thus are patent-eligible. The Office contends that under Step 2A, Prong One of the subject-matter-eligibility analysis (MPEP § 2f06.04.I.A.l), independent claims I and 24 each "fall[] within the 'mental processes' grouping of abstract ideas." Action at 9. This is because, according to the Office, the recited "'segmenting each of the 3D representation(s) into ventral and dorsal portions' can be achieved

by a user viewing a 3D image and selecting/deciding which sections represent the ventral and dorsal portions via a user interface" and "determining the mean curvature can be performed in the human mind by performing a calculation of an average ... by: 1) mental math; 2) pen/paper." Id. And the Office further contends that under Step 2A, Prong Two of the subject matter eligibility analysis (MPEP § 2106.04.ILA.2), "the claims do not recite any additional elements to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application because the claim as written does not include elements to 1) improve the functioning of a computer ... 2) effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis ... 3) use a particular machine ... [or] 4) use the judicial exceptions in a meaningful way beyond generally linking the use to a particular technological environment." Id. at 9-10. That is incorrect.
1. Prong One: The Claims Do Not Recite a Mental Process

First, the Office has not established that the recited "segment[ation of] each of the 3D representation(s)" of the data "into ventral and dorsal portions" and the "determin[ation of] a mean curvature of at least a region of a surface of the dorsal portion and/or a mean curvature of at least a region of a surface of the ventral portion" could "as a practical matter, be performed entirely in a human's mind." CyberSource Corp. v. RetailDecisions, Inc., 654 F.3d 1366, 1376 (Fed. Cir. 2011). Notably, not even the Office's explanation sets forth a way in which the recited steps could "be performed entirely in a human's mind": the Office's explanation invokes reliance on "a user interface (i.e., touchscreen, cursor, buttons, and the like)" to segment "the ventral and dorsal portions" of the 3D representation of a section of a patient's central nervous system, and as the Board has held a "user's interaction with a GUI ... is not a mental process." Action at 9; CyberSource, 654 F.3d at 1376; Ex parte Jones, Appeal No. 20 19-004559, slip op. at 10-11 (PTAB Jan. 1, 2021). The Office thus has not carried its burden to show that the claimed steps could practically be performed entirely in the human mind.
Nor could the Office make the requisite showing. In addressing the recited segmentation and mean-curvature-calculation separately, the Office "does not appreciate how

the limitations ... operate as a whole." Jones, Appeal No. 2019-004559, slip op. at 11-12. The recited segmentation of a 3D representation "into ventral and dorsal portions" is a precursor to the mean-curvature calculation, as the calculation is of the "mean curvature of at least a region of a surface of the dorsal portion" and/or "of the ventral portion" from the segmentation. Thus, input data-a 3D representation of a section of a central nervous system-is segmented and the calculation is performed for one or both of the segmented portions. This is a patent-eligible "specific manner" of performing an analysis rather than a "conventional" or "generic" image analysis, akin to other cases that involved "the manipulation of [] data structures" and "the output of a modified computer structure," which "could not, as a practical matter, be performed entirely in a human's mind." CyberSource, 654 F.3d at 1376; Jones, Appeal No. 2019- 0045589, slip op. at 11-12 (quoting Core Wireless Licensing S.A.R.L. v. LG Elecs., Inc., 880 F.3d 1356, 1363 (Fed. Cir. 2018)). Being "mindful not to exaggerate the reasonable capacity of the human mind to perform concepts as a practical matter," segmentation of data as complex as a 3D representation of a section of a central nervous system-which "can comprise data that represents the geometry of the section" like "a polyhedron whose surface is defined by a plurality of polygons"-to perform segment-specific calculations thereon exceeds what "the human mind is [] equipped to detect." Ex parte Loose, Appeal No. 2022-001026, slip op. at
15-17 (PTAB Jun. 6, 2022) (citing SRIInt'l, Inc. v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 930 F.3d 1295, 1304 (Fed. Cir. 2019)); Specification at [0047]-[0048].

Beyond that, the Office "exaggerate[s] the reasonable capacity of the human mind" in contending that the "mean curvature of at least a region of a surface" of a segment of the 3D representation "can be performed in the human mind" via "mental math" or "pen/paper," especially for a 3D representation of a structure as complex as a section of a central nervous

system. Action at 9; Loose, Appeal No. 2022-001026, slip op. at 15. The human mind is not practically equipped to determine curvature at one location-let alone multiple locations, to take a mean thereof-of such a surface. As an illustration of the types of calculations that may

be involved, when the 3D representation comprises a polyhedron, "curvature of each of the region's polygonal faces" can be determined by determining "a curvature ... for each vertex ... thereof using, for example, paraboloid fitting (e.g., with least squared residuals) or quadric fitting of a curved surface," and the curvatures of the polygonal faces can be averaged. Specification at [0052]. As another illustration, "[c]urvature calculations can also be based on Gaussian curvature and the Gauss-Bonnet theorem of angle deficit." Id. These are not the type of calculations performable entirely within the human mind. Underscoring this, the Specification does not suggest that surface curvature can be determined mentally and instead highlights the "Materialise Mimics Curvature Analysis tool" as an "illustrative program for determining a region's mean curvature." Id.
2. Prong Two: The Claimed Approach Is an Improvement to Technology

Second, the claims as a whole recite an approach that "improves another technology or technical field," demonstrating that-to the extent they recite a judicial exception (which they do not)-they "integrate[] the exception into a practical application" and are thus not "directed to" a judicial exception. MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.04(d)(1). As the Specification explains, segmenting "each of the 3D representation(s) ... into ventral and dorsal portions" and performing a "textural analysis" that includes "determining a mean curvature of at least a region of the surface of the section" can "yield information that facilitates diagnosis of neurological disorders and the assessment of the progression thereof for a wide range of patients." Specification at [0005]-[0006], [0065]. The recited segmentation of a 3D representation into ventral and dorsal portions before performing the mean-curvature calculation for at least one of the portions is thus an improvement in that it can "provide reliable metrics" that "permit more personalized assessments than prior metrics" that did not rely on such segmentation. Id. This is supported by, for example, the studies set forth in Examples 1 and 2 of the Specification.
As such, the claims are not directed to a judicial exception.
B. Step 2B: The Claims Amount to Significantly More

Furthennore, the claims "amount to significantly more than [a] judicial exception itself' because, as noted in Section V.A.2, the claimed segmentation of a 3D representation of a section of a central nervous system into ventral and dorsal portions to perform a calculation on at least one of the segmented portions is an improvement over a generic image analysis, as it "provide[s] reliable metrics" that "permit more personalized assessments than prior metrics." Specification at [0005]-[0006], [0065]; MPEP § 2106.05, 2106.05(a).
For at least these reasons, all claims are patent-eligible under § 101. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections. VI. Conclusion

The pending claims are in condition for allowance for at least the reasons set forth above. Applicant does not acquiesce to the Office's characterizations of the claim language or the cited references, and reserves the right to challenge any such characterizations in the future. The Examiner is invited to contact the undersigned attorney with any questions or comments relating to this application.
